summary: This informational RFC gives a framework for a GMPLS control plane in wavelength switched optical networks. Impairments degrade optical signals along a path, so they matter when setting up and maintaining paths.

plainLanguage.summary: Light in glass fibre gets a bit worse the farther it goes. This explains how the network plans paths with that in mind.

questions: how do wson control planes handle signal degradation
subtitle: Optical signals degrade over distance; this framework shows how networks account for it when planning paths.

tldr.problem: Light signals transmitted through optical fiber degrade as they travel distances and pass through devices. Networks that ignore these physical impairments can end up with paths so degraded the signal cannot be received properly.
tldr.mechanism: This framework describes how GMPLS control planes and Path Computation Elements can factor in optical impairments when selecting and validating routes, distinguishing transparent segments where signals can travel unaided from segments that need regeneration.
tldr.outcome: Networks can be designed more efficiently without overprovisioning regenerators at every span, and paths can be set up dynamically with confidence in signal quality.

facts.label: Main standard
facts.value: ITU-T Recommendation G.680 for impairment models

today: RFC 6566 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary framework document for impairment-aware optical networks, though no corresponding protocol standards have mandated its adoption. Vendors and operators have implemented subsets of the architectures it describes in proprietary or experimental systems.

sections.title: Wavelength Switched Optical Networks
sections.content:
A Wavelength Switched Optical Network (WSON) is built from optical fiber links and switching equipment that routes signals based on the wavelength (color) of the light. These networks use Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) to pack many separate signals onto a single fiber, each at a different wavelength. The network also includes devices like Reconfigurable Optical Add/Drop Multiplexers (ROADMs), which can direct specific wavelengths to different outputs, and wavelength converters, which shift a signal from one wavelength to another.

A WSON handles its own routing and switching through a control plane, often based on GMPLS, that sets up optical paths dynamically. The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture provides a way for specialized computation engines to plan these paths. But when these control planes were first designed, they did not account for a critical physical fact: optical signals degrade as they travel.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone company's network uses different colors of light to send many calls down one fiber at once, and switches at each junction decide which way each color goes. The switches are controlled by computers that decide on routes.

sections.title: Optical Impairments and Signal Degradation
sections.content:
As an optical signal travels through fiber and passes through devices, it experiences impairments: physical effects that degrade its quality. The most significant are chromatic dispersion (different wavelengths travel at slightly different speeds), polarization-mode dispersion (the signal splits into different states), optical nonlinearities (the signal distorts when power is high), amplified spontaneous emission (noise from optical amplifiers), and loss (the signal simply gets weaker). These impairments accumulate over the length of the path.

The degree of degradation matters because a receiver must see enough signal and low enough noise to decode the information correctly. Engineers measure this readiness as the Q-factor or Optical Signal-to-Noise Ratio (OSNR). If a path's impairments push the signal below the receiver's threshold, the connection will fail. The RFC defines transparent segments as sections where no regeneration happens, and regeneration points as places where a device converts the optical signal back to electrical, removes the accumulated impairment, and re-transmits it optically, resetting the impairment count.
sections.plainLanguage: Light gets dimmer, splits into different waves, and bounces around when it travels far through glass, making the message harder to read at the other end. Stations along the way can clean up the light and send it fresh again.

sections.title: Network Requirements and Scenarios
sections.content:
Not all optical networks need impairment-aware control planes. Some networks are designed with such generous margins that every possible path is viable. Others are under-provisioned with regenerators, or support mixed bitrates where different signal types have different tolerance for impairment. The RFC outlines four scenarios: networks that ignore impairments entirely, networks where impairments are considered only at design time, networks that use approximation techniques to estimate impairments along a path, and (future) networks that compute impairments in full detail.

A complication arises from "black links"—multi-channel fiber spans where only the single-channel interfaces are standardized and the internal details are proprietary. A vendor controlling black links may not publish impairment parameters. The framework addresses this by allowing impairment estimation to be centralized within the vendor's domain while the rest of the control plane remains distributed, or by having the vendor furnish pre-validated paths rather than impairment data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks need to think about light degradation carefully, others don't. Also, some fiber companies don't say how degraded light gets in their networks, so the control system has to work around it.

sections.title: Computation Architectures
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main ways to organize path computation when impairments matter. The first, Combined Routing, Wavelength Assignment, and Impairment Validation (IV), puts all three decisions into a single computation entity (usually a PCE), allowing optimal choices but requiring that entity to have access to all relevant impairment data. The second, IV-Candidates + RWA, separates impairment validation into one entity that provides a list of valid paths and wavelengths, and routing/wavelength assignment into another that picks the best one based on current availability. This allows the impairment expert to be isolated and specialized but introduces coordination overhead.

The third approach, Routing + Distributed IV, has the routing and wavelength assignment processes work together while impairment measures (like OSNR and dispersion) are accumulated as the signal travels along the path via signaling. Each hop adds its contribution, and the final node decides whether the path is feasible. This avoids spreading impairment data across the network but may be less optimal and harder to coordinate.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can have one computer that decides everything about a path, or split the job between one that checks for light degradation and another that picks a route, or let each station along the way report how bad the light looks so far.

sections.title: Impact on GMPLS and PCE
sections.content:
The different computation architectures place different demands on GMPLS protocols. If impairment information is distributed, routing protocols need to carry impairment characteristics of links and devices, potentially causing scaling issues due to the volume of data. Signaling protocols may need extension to carry accumulated impairment measures along a path. PCE communication protocol (PCEP) must be extended to allow PCEs to request and return impairment validation results and to coordinate between independent PCEs.

The combined IV & RWA approach requires PCEP to carry impairment data and is heaviest on the PCE computationally but simplest operationally. The IV-Candidates approach reduces the computation burden but requires coordination between two PCEs. The distributed approach avoids distributing impairment data but potentially offers less-optimal paths and requires new signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing computers and path computers need to exchange information about light quality and path feasibility. How much and what kind depends on how much work each computer is doing.
